fields.sections.0.ko: To understand life phenomena and treat disease, we must know how genomic variations affect molecular levels. However, since the human genome contains approximately 9 billion possible single-character variants, it is practically impossible to verify each one in the laboratory. To solve this problem, DeepMind developed AlphaGenome, an artificial intelligence model capable of predicting the effects of genomic variants on biological processes. While the existing AlphaGenome was useful for analyzing specific variants, researchers precomputed predictions at scale to enable researchers to see the full picture of variants across the entire genome, creating an accessible resource called AlphaGenome Atlas.
fields.sections.1.ko: AlphaGenome Atlas is a petabyte-scale dataset containing molecular effect predictions for 9 billion variants, over 30 times larger than the AlphaFold Database. This platform goes beyond a simple list of predictions and provides multiple layers of information. The AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score integrates predictions from AlphaGenome and AlphaMissense models into a single number, enabling researchers to rapidly rank variants and simultaneously interpret molecular effects. The platform is provided through an intuitive website portal, API, and Google Antigravity skills, and is freely accessible for non-profit purposes.
fields.sections.2.ko: The molecular effect prediction portion of AlphaGenome Atlas contains thousands of predictions for each variant, covering several important aspects of gene regulation across hundreds of human and mouse cell types and tissues. The AVI score represents the impact of each genetic variant as a single number, and AVI feature contributions link each score to specific molecular processes such as RNA splicing or gene expression that drive it. Additionally, it provides a comprehensive DNA sequence motif collection containing over 2,500 recurring DNA sequence patterns and their locations, supporting diverse genetic research tasks from variant ranking to in-depth variant function analysis.
fields.sections.3.ko: An important feature of AlphaGenome Atlas is that it handles not only the 2% protein-coding region of the genome but also the remaining 98% of non-coding regions that regulate gene activity and contain most trait-associated variants. Designed through broad community collaboration, the AVI score demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on multiple variant pathogenicity and rare disease benchmarks. Through AVI feature contribution calculations, researchers can interpret prediction scores, highlighting molecular processes such as RNA splicing or gene expression predicted to be most affected by each variant.
fields.sections.4.ko: A major challenge in rare disease research is finding a small number of causal variants among thousands of candidate variants. Through collaboration with the GREGoR consortium, researchers at the Broad Institute used the AVI score to discover a DNM1 gene variant previously overlooked in prior research. AlphaGenome predictions showed that this variant creates an incorrect splice site, resulting in abnormal protein extension, experimental validation confirmed this prediction, and neighboring variants with similar effects were also discovered. This demonstrates how powerful a tool AlphaGenome Atlas is for understanding impactful genomic variants.
fields.sections.5.ko: Beyond rare diseases, Gareth Hawkes at the University of Exeter applied AlphaGenome Atlas to whole-genome data from over 54,000 participants in the UK Biobank to uncover the genetic architecture of common traits in the general population. By grouping rare variants based on predicted molecular effects, an additional 22% of non-coding genetic associations buried in statistical background noise were discovered. Through this, specific regulatory variants were identified that regulate levels of important proteins such as PLA2G7 related to aging and EGLN1 essential for cellular oxygen sensing. Furthermore, Hawkes used AlphaGenome Atlas to focus on the top 1% of hundreds of millions of non-coding variants predicted to have the highest impact, confirming 19 genetic regions associated with body mass index.
fields.sections.6.ko: AlphaGenome Atlas is also utilized to identify motifs—recurring short sequence patterns that drive molecular processes of diverse genes in various cell types. These motifs become important clues for identifying binding sites of transcription factors that turn genes on and off and provide additional interpretation of non-coding variants. Julia Zeitlinger and Melanie Weilert at the Stowers Institute for Medical Research used this resource to classify transcription factors that only affect DNA accessibility from those that also have the ability to turn genes on and off.
fields.sections.7.ko: AlphaGenome Atlas is creating new layers of information to deepen our understanding of the human genetic code, but DeepMind views it not as an end but as a foundation. As artificial intelligence models like AlphaGenome improve, the complete human genome map is expected to become increasingly comprehensive and accurate. AlphaGenome Atlas will be integrated into broader agentic systems like Google Antigravity to improve end-to-end scientific workflows for biologists, accelerating progress toward discovering new therapeutic targets, understanding genetic disorders, and advancing to the next stage of targeted experimental validation.
fields.caveat: Since the currently reported content is an official announcement from Google DeepMind, independent academic validation and actual clinical application effects will need to be confirmed through subsequent peer-reviewed papers and field data.
